summary: An official status report on network numbers and gateway autonomous system numbers in the Internet. It replaces RFC 1020 and was replaced by RFC 1117 and RFC 1166.

eli5.summary: It is a list of who has which network numbers, kept up to date as the Internet grew.

questions: where were network numbers listed in 1988
how are ip addresses divided into classes
subtitle: The official registry of IP network numbers and autonomous system numbers in use on the Internet.

tldr.problem: The growing Internet needs a central registry of which organizations own which network numbers and autonomous systems to prevent conflicts and enable routing.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Network Information Center (NIC) maintains and publishes lists of assigned network numbers (for Class A, B, and C networks) and autonomous system numbers, organized by category (Research, Defense, Government, Commercial).
tldr.outcome: Network administrators can request numbers from a central authority, and routing tables can be built based on authoritative number assignments. This document was replaced by RFC 1117 and RFC 1166.

today: RFC 1062 was replaced by RFC 1117 and RFC 1166 as the Internet continued to grow. The centralized network number registry evolved into today's Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) that allocate IP address space. The class-based addressing scheme was later supplemented by Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) to make more efficient use of the limited IPv4 address space.

sections.title: What This Document Does
sections.content:
This RFC is an official status report documenting all network numbers and gateway autonomous system numbers currently assigned in the Internet community. The Internet Protocol (IP) uses 32-bit addresses divided into a network part and a local address part. As the Internet grew, multiple organizations needed network numbers, and the NIC (Network Information Center) at SRI International became the authority for assigning and tracking these numbers.

The document is periodically updated, with current information available from the Hostmaster at the DDN Network Information Center. Each entry lists the network number, the organization responsible for it, contact information, and references to relevant protocol specifications. The NIC maintains this registry to prevent conflicts and provide authoritative information for routing decisions.
sections.eli5: This is like a phone book for the Internet that says which company owns which network address range and how to contact them if there are questions.

sections.title: IP Address Classes and Notation
sections.content:
IP addresses are 32 bits divided into a network part and a local address part. The division takes four forms or classes. Class A has a 7-bit network number and 24-bit local address (high bit is 0), allowing 128 networks. Class B has a 14-bit network number and 16-bit local address (high 2 bits are 10), allowing 16,384 networks. Class C has a 21-bit network number and 8-bit local address (high 3 bits are 110), allowing 2,097,152 networks. Class D is for multicast addresses (high 4 bits are 1110). Class E (high 4 bits are 1111) is reserved for future use.

The standard notation for IP addresses divides them into four 8-bit fields expressed as decimal numbers separated by periods, called dotted decimal notation (for example, 10.1.0.52). Special addresses include 0 meaning "this network", all ones meaning "all hosts", and network 127 reserved for loopback (datagrams sent there never appear on any actual network).
sections.eli5: IP addresses have a class (A, B, C, D) that determines the split between the network number and the computer number. The numbers are written with dots, like 10.1.0.52.

sections.title: Network Categories and Assignment Policies
sections.content:
Networks are assigned to one of four user categories: Research (R), Defense (D), Government (G), and Commercial (C). The category code appears at the left margin of each network entry. Research networks are typically at universities and research institutions, Defense networks support military operations, Government networks serve civilian government agencies, and Commercial networks are owned by companies and service providers.

Independent networks that use IP protocols but are not connected to the research or operational Internet are marked with an asterisk. These independent networks must apply separately for permission to interconnect with the Internet. For various reasons, assigned network numbers are sometimes changed. During transition periods, old numbers are listed with a "T" suffix and a "-TEMP" suffix on the network name to ease migration to the new number.
sections.eli5: Networks are labeled by category: R for research universities, D for defense, G for government, and C for commercial companies. This shows what type of organization uses each network.

sections.title: Class A and Class B Networks
sections.content:
Class A networks (1 through 126) include major research networks like ARPANET (network 10) and MILNET (network 26), as well as commercial networks like ATT (network 12) and XEROX-NET (network 13). Network 0 is reserved, network 127 is reserved for loopback. Class A networks are rare because each one accommodates millions of hosts, so they are assigned only to very large organizations and networks.

Class B networks provide moderate size (up to 65,534 hosts each) and are more commonly assigned. Examples include CMU-NET (128.2), RUTGERS (128.6), PURDUE-NET (128.46), and many university and research institution networks. The registry documents hundreds of Class B assignments to universities, government facilities, companies, and research networks worldwide, each with contact information for the responsible administrator.
sections.eli5: Class A networks are given to the biggest organizations (like ARPANET and MILNET). Class B networks are given to large universities and research centers. Each network in the list has a contact person.

sections.title: Network Number Allocation and Governance
sections.content:
The Hostmaster at the DDN Network Information Center receives requests for network numbers and assigns them according to organizational size and expected growth. The NIC maintains authority to prevent duplicate assignments and ensure that the global Internet routing tables can be built correctly. Network numbers are not reused, and the allocation process requires justification of network size needs.

The protocol conventions documented in this and related RFCs specify that numbers be expressed in decimal and data in "big-endian" order (most significant octet first). The NIC WHOIS/NICNAME service allows anyone to look up network ownership and contact information. As the Internet grew, the demand for network numbers eventually exceeded the supply of Class A and B addresses, leading to the development of Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) to allocate addresses more efficiently.
sections.eli5: The NIC is like a registry office that hands out network numbers to organizations that need them. You can look up who owns each network, and the numbers follow strict rules about how they are divided.
